we-the-people-1787-1791.works: The 1790 pies read well from the projector: blue and orange-red are bold, and Virginia's big half-orange pie answers 'most people' at a glance. Each state's pop-up holds every number for Q1 to Q3 in one place, and the House seats shading with its 'VA: 19' style labels lets me point to the biggest states without clicking.

findings.where: q2-seats view; House seats in 1793 turned on, with Ratifying the Constitution pies and labels also showing; Seats in Congress, steps 1-2
findings.what: I turn on House seats and the screen also shows the ratification pies and their order labels, so 'NY: 10' sits next to 'NY 11', 'PA: 13' near 'PA 2', 'VA: 19' near 'VA 10', and 'NC: 10' between 'NC (1788)' and 'NC 12'. The legend doesn't list the ratification layer, and the layer list says it should be off.
findings.why: From the projector, the class copies numbers off the screen. Half of them will write that Pennsylvania had 2 seats or Virginia 10, and I can't sort it out without explaining a layer we haven't reached yet.
findings.suggestion: Check why Ratifying the Constitution draws when House seats in 1793 is turned on (its saved visibility, or the seats layer carrying those labels). Then make the two label sets impossible to confuse: 'VA 19 seats' on the House layer and 'VA 10th' on the ratification layer.

findings.where: q2-seats view; House seats in 1793 labels; Seats in Congress, step 2 and the 'fewest' part of the answer
findings.what: Only seven seat labels show: NY: 10, CT: 7, PA: 13, KY: 2, VA: 19, NC: 10 and GA: 2. Delaware, New Jersey, Maryland, South Carolina, New Hampshire, Vermont and Rhode Island have no label, and Massachusetts is under the pop-up. Delaware, the answer for 'fewest', is a tiny pale state with nothing on it.
findings.why: Reading the labels is what makes this question work from one screen or a printout. Without 'DE: 1', the class will answer Kentucky or Georgia (2), and zooming around to find it uses up a 15-minute slot.
findings.suggestion: Let the seat labels draw even when they crowd (turn off label deconfliction for this layer, or give it priority over other labels), use a smaller font for small states, and add to step 2: 'Open the New England and New York bookmark to read the small states.'

findings.where: q4-ratify view; Ratifying the Constitution pies and labels; How close was ratification?, steps 3-4
findings.what: Each label sits up and to the right of its pie, so it lands on the next pie. 'NC (1788)' is printed across Virginia's pie, 'VA 10' sits just under Delaware's, and 'NC 12' sits beside the orange Hillsborough pie. MA 6, CT 5, NJ 3 and DE 1 don't show at all, and Massachusetts' big pie covers Rhode Island's and New Hampshire's.
findings.why: When I send a student up to click North Carolina's two pies, they'll click the one with 'NC (1788)' on it and get Virginia. Massachusetts is one of the three closest votes, and at this zoom you can't tell which pie is its.
findings.suggestion: Center each label just below its pie (or on it, with a halo). Add to the sheet: 'Open The South bookmark to find North Carolina's two pies' and 'Open the New England and New York bookmark for the New England votes.'

findings.where: open and q1-virginia views; Population in 1790 pies and pop-up first line; Who lived where in 1790?, step 3
findings.what: The pies have no labels, so the percentage enslaved appears only in the pop-ups, and there it reads '39.099998474121094%'. North Carolina is right at a quarter, so its pie alone doesn't settle whether it's over 25%.
findings.why: From the front I'd be clicking 15 pies one at a time, and pairs working from paper with no device can't do the second half of Q1 at all. Students will copy the long decimal or ask what it means.
findings.suggestion: Round the percentage in the pop-up to a whole number or one decimal place. Add a small label to each pie such as 'VA 39%', so one projected view or a printed screenshot answers Q1.

findings.where: Population / House seats pop-up (q1-virginia, q2-seats); The three-fifths clause, step 2
findings.what: The sheet says the 'counted in full / not at all' seats are in the last two lines. In fact the pop-up ends with the Kentucky or Maine note and 'Seats: National Archives · Ratio: U.S. Census Bureau'. The numbers are in the third paragraph, and in the pop-up box you scroll past them to reach the end.
findings.why: Students scroll to the bottom, find the sources line and put their hands up, all at the same moment.
findings.suggestion: Change step 2 to 'read the paragraph that starts If enslaved people had been counted in full', or move that paragraph to the end of the pop-up so 'last two lines' is true.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text for Virginia and Massachusetts: the 'If enslaved people had been counted in full' paragraph is followed by two more paragraphs

findings.where: q4-nc view; Population in 1790 pies showing alongside Ratifying the Constitution pies; How close was ratification?, steps 1-3
findings.what: In the North Carolina picture, the light-blue and orange-red 1790 population pies are still showing next to the darker blue and orange-red ratification pies. Blue means 'free people' on one and 'voted to ratify' on the other.
findings.why: If a pair misses step 1, or a slow Chromebook lags on the toggle, they're reading two sets of pies in the same colors and can't tell which is which.
findings.suggestion: Give the ratification pies their own colors (for example green for ratify and purple for against) and change the sheet's Reading the map line to match.

rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-liv.works: This one suits a single projected screen: the whole class shares one town, and the district pop-up is one clean line giving the name, party and district number. The historic-place pop-up turned out to give the building's name and type as well as the address, so we don't need the National Archives link, which our filter may block.

findings.where: open view and the app's tool list; whole map; Who represents us?, step 1, and every later question
findings.what: The map opens on all of North America, and the tools list has no search box. Every pair has to pinch and drag from the whole continent down to our neighborhood.
findings.why: On phones and shared Chromebooks that takes several minutes before anyone reads a pop-up, and Q1 has 15 minutes of a 45-minute period.
findings.suggestion: Add the Search tool to the app so students can type the town or the school's address, or give teachers a one-line how-to for saving a copy of the map with a bookmark for their own town.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--open.png; tools list in the packet (Basemaps, Map layers, Legend, Measure, Sketch, 2D/3D, Bookmarks)

findings.where: zoomed-out state view; Congressional districts (119th Congress); Who represents us?, step 4
findings.what: To answer 'how many districts does your state have?' we have to count blue outlines. Zoomed out, state lines and district lines are the same blue, and the city districts shrink to slivers.
findings.why: Counting 15 shapes for Ohio off a projector is slow, and someone always gets 14 or 16. For a big state it can't be done.
findings.suggestion: Add the state's total to the pop-up, for example '... represents Ohio Congressional District 15, one of Ohio's 15 districts', or draw state boundaries in a heavier line than district boundaries.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--open.png; q1-district pop-up text 'Mike Carey (Republican) represents Ohio Congressional District 15'

findings.where: q4-nrhp and q4-nrhp-click; National Register of Historic Places pop-up; History where we live, step 3, and Reading the map
findings.what: The sheet says the pop-up gives an address but not a name, yet the one I opened is titled 'Ohio Statehouse'. At the zoom where the diamonds appear, the basemap shows streets, parks and neighborhoods but no building names under the diamonds.
findings.why: That's good news with our filter, because students don't need the National Archives link. But the sheet sends them to a basemap label that isn't there and a link they don't need.
findings.suggestion: Reword Reading the map and step 3: 'The pop-up title gives the place's name; if it doesn't, use the address.' Keep the National Archive Information link as optional.

findings.where: q4-nrhp and q4-nrhp-click; National Register of Historic Places diamonds; History where we live, steps 2-3
findings.what: The diamond that opened 'Ohio Statehouse' (1 of 2) sits on South High Street by the I-70 overpass, at the edge of the Brewery District. That's roughly half a mile south of Capitol Square at High and Broad, where the 'Columbus' label is.
findings.why: If diamonds sit that far from their buildings, 'click the two nearest your school' and 'read the label under the diamond' send students to the wrong building, and I'd be correcting it live in front of the class.
findings.suggestion: Check how the National Register points are placed, and whether some sit on a reference point rather than on the building. If many are off, tell students to trust the pop-up's name and address over where the diamond sits.

findings.where: q4-nrhp legend and diamonds; National Register of Historic Places; History where we live, step 4
findings.what: District (rust) and site (dark red) look alike, structure and object are pale diamonds on a pale basemap, and every diamond is small on the projector.
findings.why: From the back of the room nobody can tell a district from a site by color. The pop-up's 'Resource Type' line is the reliable answer.
findings.suggestion: Change step 4 to 'read Resource Type in the pop-up', and give each type its own shape and a slightly larger size.

findings.where: Sketch tool and the app's tool list; Rights in public places and Responsibilities (Q2-Q3)
findings.what: Q2 and Q3 only work on a device with Sketch, and the sketches disappear when the map closes. There's no Print tool, so I can't give pairs without a Chromebook a printed map of our downtown to mark by hand.
findings.why: When the cart is short, a third of the class needs a paper route. The basemap at building-label zoom would make a good handout.
findings.suggestion: Add the Print tool (or an export-to-image option) to the app, so the teacher can print the town view at building-label zoom for pairs to mark with a pencil.
findings.evidence: Tools list in the packet; Reading the map: 'Sketches are not saved when you close the map'

presidential-elections-1796-1800.works: The orange and blue pies are bold and big enough to read from the back, and switching 1796 off and 1800 on at the front shows the New York flip as one clear moment. Pop-up titles give the state and its electors, and the McCulloch pop-up fits its Why here on one screen.

findings.where: q4-marbury view (zoomed to Washington and Baltimore); Landmark Supreme Court cases; The Supreme Court, near the capital, steps 1-2
findings.what: I click the Marbury v. Madison square and nothing opens. McCulloch's square does open, Why here and all.
findings.why: Half the question is 'what happened in each place'. Without Marbury's pop-up the class has nothing to read, and I end up telling them the answer.
findings.suggestion: Check that the Marbury feature has its pop-up turned on and that it opens at the zoomed-in scale. Try clicking the square itself, not the label, and if the click target is the problem, make the squares a little larger.

findings.where: open and q1-pie views; Supreme Court squares drawn over the Election of 1796 pies; The election of 1796, step 3; The election of 1800, steps 2-3; Supreme Court, step 1
findings.what: At the sixteen-states view, the two pink squares sit on top of Maryland's pie. That hides Maryland's split, the only split state Adams won in 1796 and the 5-5 tie in 1800. The McCulloch label doesn't show, the two squares overlap each other, and the sheet's Supreme Court steps never say to zoom in.
findings.why: On the projector the class can't see Maryland's two colors, and a click there may open a court case instead. With the squares overlapping, measuring between them is guesswork.
findings.suggestion: Make the Supreme Court layer draw only when zoomed in past the sixteen-states scale, and add a 'Washington and Baltimore' bookmark. Add 'Zoom in on the two pink squares near the capital' (as From the front has it) as step 1 of the sheet's Supreme Court question.

findings.where: q2-1800 view; pop-up left open while switching layers; The election of 1800, steps 1-3; Which states switched?, step 1
findings.what: After I switch to 1800, the Pennsylvania pop-up is still open and still reads 'Electors' votes in 1796: John Adams 1, Thomas Jefferson 14 ...'. Its title is only 'Pennsylvania: 15 electors', with no year.
findings.why: Students will copy 1796 numbers into the 1800 answer. While I toggle back and forth for Q3, any pop-up left open shows the wrong year half the time.
findings.suggestion: Put the year in every pop-up title ('Pennsylvania in 1800: 15 electors'), and add 'Close any open pop-up first' to the sheet's layer-switching steps.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q2-1800.png (1800 layer on, pop-up showing the 1796 votes)

findings.where: q2-1800 view; Election of 1800 pies; Which states switched?, step 2
findings.what: In the 1800 picture, New York's pie is a solid olive green that isn't in the legend, and Pennsylvania's has a green section. It looks as if the 1796 orange and the 1800 blue were drawn on top of each other while the layers switched.
findings.why: New York turning from orange to blue is the whole answer to Q3. If the class sees a green pie, that moment is spoiled.
findings.suggestion: Check that once the switch finishes, New York is solid blue and only one election's pies show. If the two layers can show together, consider labels such as 'NY 1800' on the pies, or one layer with a 1796/1800 choice.

findings.where: open view; Election of 1796 and 1800 pies; questions 1-3
findings.what: The pies carry no state names or elector counts, so every split has to be found by clicking.
findings.why: Pairs without a device could compare printed 1796 and 1800 screenshots if each pie said 'MD 10'. Right now a printout shows colors with no names.
findings.suggestion: Label each pie with the state's abbreviation and electors (for example 'MD 10'), sized to read on a projector.

louisiana-purchase-1803-1806.works: The yellow purchase beside the older United States reads at a glance from the projector, and one click gives both fill-in numbers (530 million acres, $15 million) in one sentence. The Missouri Region pop-up names the basin in big type, and the Across the Rockies bookmark clearly shows the trail leaving the yellow and the unshaded Pacific Northwest.

findings.where: q3-biomes (Up the Missouri bookmark, Biomes on) and q3-biome-click; Biomes and United States Watersheds; Up the Missouri, steps 3-4
findings.what: At the Up the Missouri bookmark with Biomes on, there's no biome shading: the route is the same pale yellow as the purchase. The brown watershed outlines are still there, and a click opened 'Souris-Red-Rainy Region, HUC ID: 09' (1 of 3). The biome pop-up only appeared after zooming out to the whole country.
findings.why: Students who follow the sheet exactly will write a watershed name as the biome. From the front, I'd have to know to zoom out and to arrow through the pop-ups.
findings.suggestion: Check the Biomes layer's visible range (it may switch off at closer zooms) and how long it takes to draw on a slow connection. Check that turning off United States Watersheds hides all its HUC sublayers. If Biomes only draws zoomed out, set the Up the Missouri bookmark one level further out, or change step 4 to 'zoom out until the biome shading appears'.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biomes.png (route pixels identical to the purchase yellow; watershed pop-up 'Souris-Red-Rainy Region HUC ID: 09', 1 of 3); louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biome-click.png

findings.where: open, q1-purchase and q2-missouri-basin views; Territorial acquisitions to 1803; A bigger country, steps 1-3
findings.what: On screen, the 1783 land is a dark grey-teal, not what my students would call green. When I click the Louisiana Purchase, the highlight turns the yellow purchase bright green.
findings.why: On the projector, just as I'm saying 'green is the 1783 land', the purchase turns green. The back rows will mix them up.
findings.suggestion: Give the 1783 land a fill with an easy color name that won't clash with the highlight (for example light grey), or change the sheet to 'dark grey-green'. Use an outline-only highlight if the app allows it.

findings.where: q1-purchase and q3-biome-click views (eastern end of the trail); Lewis and Clark trail and campsites; Why New Orleans?, step 3; Across the Rockies, steps 3-4
findings.what: Nothing on the map names New Orleans or Pittsburgh. The trail line ends in western Pennsylvania, but a scatter of campsite dots carries on east toward the Chesapeake, so 'the trail's eastern end' isn't obvious.
findings.why: A student who starts Measure at the easternmost dot will probably get a distance above the accepted 2,100 to 2,300 miles. 'Which city sits near the mouth' depends on what they already know, and on paper there's nothing to go on.
findings.suggestion: Add a small labeled reference layer with Pittsburgh, St. Louis, New Orleans and the mouth of the Columbia. Check what the dots east of Pittsburgh are (perhaps Lewis's travels before the expedition set out), and either remove them or say what they are on the sheet.

findings.where: q3-biomes legend; Biomes; Up the Missouri, step 4
findings.what: In the Biomes legend, Mangroves and Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands have exactly the same khaki swatch, and that khaki is close to the purchase yellow.
findings.why: A student who checks the legend instead of the pop-up can't tell grassland from mangrove.
findings.suggestion: Give Mangroves a different color, and keep the sheet's instruction to read the first line of the pop-up.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biomes.png (both legend swatches are the same color)

war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine.works: At The War of 1812 bookmark, the three clusters of fighting (Great Lakes, Chesapeake, Gulf Coast) stand out from across the room, and the blue and red diamonds sized by casualties make the biggest battles easy to point to. The Florida, treaty-line and recognition pop-ups are short and give exactly what the sheet asks for.

findings.where: q4-latin view; Latin American independence and US recognition labels; New nations and the Monroe Doctrine, steps 3-4
findings.what: 'Paraguay 1811' is printed right beside Brazil's blue circle, while Paraguay's own orange diamond sits further left. 'Federation of Central America 1821' runs across Haiti's orange diamond. An italic 'Peru' from the 1800 layer also sits in the middle of the continent, away from the 'Peru 1821' diamond. At laptop size, Brazil's circle and label are behind the legend.
findings.why: From the projector, students match each name to the nearest symbol, so they'll call Paraguay blue and Central America orange. That's exactly the sorting the question tests.
findings.suggestion: Place each label directly below its symbol, and add the recognition year to the label (for example 'Chile 1818, recognized 1823'), so one projected view or a printout carries the answer.

findings.where: q3-boundary and q3-treatyline views; Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819; Florida and a new border, steps 1-4
findings.what: The 1819 boundary bookmark frames the West. Florida's green land is at the far right edge, behind the legend at laptop size, and so is the Sabine River part of the line. The seven parts have no numbers on the map, and at the zoom where the short Sabine part shows, the big New Orleans diamond and other battle diamonds sit right beside it.
findings.why: I want to click parts 1 to 7 in order from the front. Without numbers I'm hunting for them, and a click near the Sabine can open a battle instead.
findings.suggestion: Reframe the bookmark to cover the whole line from the Gulf to the Pacific plus Florida, and label each dashed part with its number (1 to 7). Add 'turn off Battles of the War of 1812' to step 2, or draw the line above the battle diamonds.

findings.where: q2-neworleans pop-up; Battles of the War of 1812; Reading the map ('the pop-up's leaders and story tell you who fought'); Where was the war fought?
findings.what: The New Orleans pop-up gives the date, 'American Side Victory', the casualties and a long story, but no State Name and no leaders line, and its last paragraph is printed twice. The sheet says the leaders tell you who fought, and From the front says to read the State Name.
findings.why: For battles named after a fort or a creek, students won't know the state, or that the other side was a Native nation, unless they read the whole story, and that's a long scroll on a phone.
findings.suggestion: Add two short lines near the top of each battle pop-up: 'Where: [state]' and 'Fought: United States against [British / Red Stick Creeks / Shawnee-led confederacy]', and remove the repeated paragraph. Check that the Tippecanoe, Fort Mims and Horseshoe Bend pop-ups say who fought.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text for New Orleans (the paragraph 'On January 8, 1815, Maj. Gen. Andrew Jackson's hastily assembled army...' appears twice; no state or leaders line)

findings.where: Legend, Battles of the War of 1812 size key; open and q1-bookmark views
findings.what: The smallest step in the casualties size key reads '< 0'.
findings.why: Someone will ask how a battle had fewer than zero casualties. It's a small distraction, but it happens every period.
findings.suggestion: Set the size key's smallest step to a real value (for example 'under 50').

findings.where: q4-circle pop-up; Latin American independence and US recognition; New nations and the Monroe Doctrine, step 4
findings.what: The recognition date reads '1/27/1823, 12:00 AM'.
findings.why: Students are comparing it with 'December 2, 1823' written on the board. The time is clutter, and a written-out date is easier to compare.
findings.suggestion: Format the date as 'January 27, 1823' with no time, here and in the We the People ratification pop-ups ('11/21/1789, 12:00 AM').
findings.evidence: Pop-up text: 'Recognized by the United States: 1/27/1823, 12:00 AM.'
